First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (3-5s)^{-2/3}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, we let  $u=3-5s.$ Then differentiating with respect to $s$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}s}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}s=-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3-5s)^{-2/3}\,\text{d}s & =\int {u}^{-2/3}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{1/3}{u}^{1/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}{u}^{1/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}(3-5s)^{1/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\sqrt[3]{3-5s}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[-\frac{3}{5}\sqrt[3]{3-5s}+C] & =-\frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[\sqrt[3]{3-5s}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[(3-5s)^{1/3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3}(3-5s)^{-2/3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(3-5s)+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}(3-5s)^{-2/3}\cdot (-5) \\  & =(3-5s)^{-2/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{(3-5s)^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
